stem: How is a pinnately compound leaf different from a palmately compound leaf?
solution:
In both, the incisions of the lamina reach up to the midrib, breaking it into a number of **leaflets**, and a bud is present in the axil of the petiole but not in the axil of the leaflets. They differ in how the leaflets are attached:

| Basis of difference | Pinnately compound leaf | Palmately compound leaf |
|---|---|---|
| Attachment of leaflets | A number of leaflets are present on a common axis, the **rachis** | The leaflets are attached at a **common point**, i.e., at the tip of the petiole |
| Rachis | Present; it represents the midrib of the leaf | Absent; leaflets arise from one point |
| Example | Neem | Silk cotton |
groundedIn: §5.3.2; Fig. 5.5 — compound leaf: incisions reach the midrib; bud in axil of petiole, not of leaflets; pinnately compound: leaflets on a common axis, the rachis, representing the midrib (neem); palmately compound: leaflets attached at a common point at the tip of the petiole (silk cotton)

stem: Explain with suitable examples the different types of phyllotaxy.
solution:
**Phyllotaxy** is the pattern of arrangement of leaves on the stem or branch. It is usually of three types:

1. **Alternate:** a single leaf arises at each node in an alternate manner. Examples: china rose, mustard and sun flower.
2. **Opposite:** a pair of leaves arises at each node and the two leaves lie opposite to each other. Examples: Calotropis and guava.
3. **Whorled:** more than two leaves arise at a node and form a whorl. Example: Alstonia.
groundedIn: §5.3.3; Fig. 5.6 — phyllotaxy is the pattern of arrangement of leaves on the stem; alternate (china rose, mustard, sun flower), opposite (Calotropis, guava), whorled (Alstonia)

solution: **Aestivation** is the mode of arrangement of sepals or petals in the floral bud with respect to the other members of the same whorl. Its main types are valvate, twisted, imbricate and vexillary.
groundedIn: §5.5.1; Fig. 5.11 — aestivation: mode of arrangement of sepals or petals in floral bud with respect to other members of the same whorl; valvate, twisted, imbricate, vexillary

solution: **Placentation** is the arrangement of ovules within the ovary. Its types include marginal, axile, parietal, free central and basal.
groundedIn: §5.5.1; Fig. 5.12 — placentation: the arrangement of ovules within the ovary; marginal, axile, parietal, free central and basal

solution: A flower is **actinomorphic** (radial symmetry) when it can be divided into two equal radial halves in any radial plane passing through its centre, e.g., mustard, datura, chilli.
groundedIn: §5.5 — actinomorphic (radial symmetry): divisible into two equal radial halves in any radial plane passing through the centre; mustard, datura, chilli

solution: A flower is **zygomorphic** (bilateral symmetry) when it can be divided into two similar halves only in one particular vertical plane, e.g., pea, gulmohur, bean, Cassia.
groundedIn: §5.5 — zygomorphic (bilateral symmetry): divisible into two similar halves only in one particular vertical plane; pea, gulmohur, bean, Cassia

solution: An ovary is **superior** when the gynoecium occupies the highest position on the thalamus and the other floral parts (calyx, corolla and androecium) are situated below it, as in a **hypogynous** flower, e.g., mustard, china rose and brinjal.
groundedIn: §5.5; Fig. 5.9 — in the hypogynous flower the gynoecium occupies the highest position, other parts below it; the ovary is said to be superior (mustard, china rose, brinjal)

solution: A **perigynous flower** is one in which the gynoecium is situated in the centre and the other parts of the flower are located on the rim of the thalamus almost at the same level. The ovary here is said to be **half inferior**, e.g., plum, rose, peach.
groundedIn: §5.5; Fig. 5.9 — perigynous: gynoecium in the centre, other parts on the rim of the thalamus almost at the same level; ovary half inferior (plum, rose, peach)

solution: A stamen is **epipetalous** when it is attached to the petals, as in brinjal.
groundedIn: §5.5.1 — when stamens are attached to the petals, they are epipetalous as in brinjal

solution:
| Basis of difference | Racemose inflorescence | Cymose inflorescence |
|---|---|---|
| Growth of main axis | The main axis **continues to grow** | The main axis **terminates in a flower**, hence is limited in growth |
| Position of flowers | Flowers are borne **laterally** on the axis | The apex of the axis itself develops into a flower |
| Order of flowers | **Acropetal** succession (older flowers lower, younger towards the apex) | **Basipetal** order |
groundedIn: §5.4; Fig. 5.7; Fig. 5.8 — racemose: main axis continues to grow, flowers borne laterally in acropetal succession; cymose: main axis terminates in a flower, limited in growth, flowers borne in basipetal order

solution:
Both terms apply when the gynoecium has more than one carpel.

| Basis of difference | Apocarpous | Syncarpous |
|---|---|---|
| Condition of carpels | Carpels are **free** | Carpels are **fused** |
| Examples | Lotus and rose | Mustard and tomato |
groundedIn: §5.5.1 — when more than one carpel is present, they may be free (lotus, rose), apocarpous, or fused (mustard, tomato), syncarpous

context: Draw the labelled diagram of the following:
solution:
Gram is a **dicotyledonous, non-endospermous** seed. The labelled diagram has two views:

1. **External view of the seed:** the outer covering, the **seed coat** (outer testa and inner tegmen); on one side a scar, the **hilum**, through which the seed was attached to the fruit; just above the hilum a small pore, the **micropyle**.
2. **Seed coat removed (embryo opened out):** two large, fleshy **cotyledons** full of reserve food, attached to a short **embryonal axis**; at one end of the axis the **plumule** (towards the cotyledons' junction, the future shoot) and at the other end the **radicle** (the future root).

No endosperm is drawn, since it is absent in mature gram seeds.

Labels a marker looks for: seed coat, hilum, micropyle, cotyledon, plumule, radicle.
groundedIn: §5.7.1; Fig. 5.14; §5.7 — seed coat (testa and tegmen), hilum, micropyle above the hilum, embryo of an embryonal axis and two fleshy cotyledons, radicle and plumule at its two ends; gram seeds are non-endospermous and have two cotyledons

context: Draw the labelled diagram of the following:
solution:
The V.S. of a maize seed (a monocotyledonous, endospermic seed) is drawn as an elongated oval grain:

1. **Seed coat & fruit-wall:** the thin outermost boundary, the membranous seed coat fused with the fruit wall.
2. **Aleurone layer:** a thin proteinous layer just inside it, the outer covering of the endosperm, separating the endosperm from the embryo.
3. **Endosperm:** the bulky food-storing tissue occupying most of the grain.
4. **Embryo:** small, situated in a groove at one end of the endosperm, consisting of:
   (a) **Scutellum:** the one large, shield-shaped cotyledon lying against the endosperm.
   (b) **Plumule** enclosed in its sheath, the **coleoptile** (towards the upper side of the embryo).
   (c) **Radicle** enclosed in its sheath, the **coleorhiza** (towards the lower end).

Labels a marker looks for: seed coat & fruit-wall, aleurone layer, endosperm, embryo, scutellum, coleoptile, plumule, radicle, coleorhiza.
groundedIn: §5.7.2; Fig. 5.15 — maize: seed coat membranous and fused with fruit wall; bulky endosperm; proteinous aleurone layer; embryo in a groove at one end; scutellum; plumule and radicle enclosed in coleoptile and coleorhiza

subtopic: Description of a Flowering Plant and Its Families
stem: Take one flower of the family Solanaceae and write its semi-technical description. Also draw their floral diagram.
solution:
**Semi-technical description of Solanum nigrum (makoi), family Solanaceae (the 'potato family')**

**Vegetative characters**

1. **Habit:** herb (the family has mostly herbs, shrubs and rarely small trees).
2. **Root:** tap root system, as in most dicotyledonous plants.
3. **Stem:** herbaceous, aerial, erect, cylindrical, branched, hairy or glabrous.
4. **Leaves:** alternate, simple, exstipulate; venation reticulate.

**Floral characters**

1. **Inflorescence:** cymose (solitary or axillary in other members).
2. **Flower:** bisexual, actinomorphic.
3. **Calyx:** sepals five, united (gamosepalous), persistent; valvate aestivation.
4. **Corolla:** petals five, united (gamopetalous); valvate aestivation.
5. **Androecium:** stamens five, **epipetalous**.
6. **Gynoecium:** bicarpellary, obliquely placed, syncarpous; ovary **superior**, bilocular; placenta swollen with many ovules; **axile** placentation.
7. **Fruit:** berry. **Seeds:** many, endospermous.

**Floral formula:** \(\oplus\) (followed by the bisexual sign) \(\text{K}_{(5)}\ \overline{\text{C}_{(5)}\ \text{A}_{5}}\ \underline{\text{G}}_{(2)}\)

Here \(\oplus\) stands for actinomorphic, the brackets for fusion, the line over C and A for adhesion (epipetalous stamens), and the line under G for a superior ovary.

**Floral diagram:** the symbol \(\oplus\) is written at the top. Drawn in successive whorls from outside: an outer whorl of **five united sepals** (valvate), then **five united petals** (valvate), then **five stamens** drawn inside the corolla and joined to the petals (epipetalous); in the centre the **bicarpellary, bilocular ovary** with an oblique septum and **swollen axile placentas** bearing many ovules.

The book prints "bicarpellary obligately placed"; the intended term is obliquely placed.
groundedIn: §5.9; Fig. 5.17; §5.8; §5.1; §5.3.1 — Solanaceae: habit, stem, leaves, inflorescence, flower, calyx, corolla, androecium, gynoecium, fruit, seeds and floral formula; Solanum nigrum floral diagram; semi-technical description sequence and floral diagram/formula conventions; tap root in most dicots; reticulate venation

stem: Describe the various types of placentations found in flowering plants.
solution:
**Placentation** is the arrangement of ovules within the ovary. The main types are:

1. **Marginal:** the placenta forms a ridge along the ventral suture of the ovary and the ovules are borne on this ridge, forming two rows. Example: pea.
2. **Axile:** the placenta is axial and the ovules are attached to it in a **multilocular** ovary. Examples: china rose, tomato and lemon.
3. **Parietal:** the ovules develop on the inner wall of the ovary or on its peripheral part. The ovary is one-chambered but becomes two-chambered due to the formation of a **false septum**. Examples: mustard and Argemone.
4. **Free central:** the ovules are borne on a central axis and **septa are absent**. Examples: Dianthus and Primrose.
5. **Basal:** the placenta develops at the **base** of the ovary and a **single ovule** is attached to it. Examples: sunflower, marigold.
groundedIn: §5.5.1; Fig. 5.12 — placentation: marginal (pea), axile (china rose, tomato, lemon), parietal with false septum (mustard, Argemone), free central (Dianthus, Primrose), basal with single ovule (sunflower, marigold)

stem: What is a flower? Describe the parts of a typical angiosperm flower.
solution:
A **flower** is a **modified shoot** in which the shoot apical meristem changes to floral meristem; the internodes do not elongate and the axis is condensed, bearing floral appendages instead of leaves. It is the **reproductive unit** of angiosperms, meant for sexual reproduction.

A typical flower has four whorls arranged successively on the swollen end of the stalk (**pedicel**), called the **thalamus** or receptacle:

1. **Calyx:** the outermost whorl; its members, the **sepals**, are generally green and leaf like and protect the flower in the bud stage. It may be gamosepalous (sepals united) or polysepalous (sepals free).
2. **Corolla:** made of **petals**, usually brightly coloured to attract insects for pollination; gamopetalous or polypetalous.
3. **Androecium:** made of **stamens**, the male reproductive organs. Each stamen has a filament and an anther; the anther is usually bilobed, each lobe with two pollen-sacs in which pollen grains are produced.
4. **Gynoecium:** the female reproductive part, made of one or more **carpels**. Each carpel has a **stigma** (receptive surface for pollen), a **style** and an **ovary** bearing ovules on a placenta.

Calyx and corolla are **accessory organs**; androecium and gynoecium are **reproductive organs**. Where calyx and corolla are not distinct, as in lily, they are called **perianth**.
groundedIn: §5.4; §5.5; §5.5.1; Fig. 5.10 — a flower is a modified shoot (shoot apical meristem changes to floral meristem); reproductive unit of angiosperms; four whorls on the thalamus; calyx, corolla, androecium, gynoecium; accessory and reproductive organs; perianth in lily

stem: Define the term inflorescence. Explain the basis for the different types inflorescence in flowering plants.
solution:
**Inflorescence** is the arrangement of flowers on the floral axis.

**Basis of classification:** whether the **apex** of the main axis gets developed into a flower or continues to grow. On this basis, two major types are defined:

1. **Racemose inflorescence:** the main axis **continues to grow** and the flowers are borne laterally in an **acropetal succession**.
2. **Cymose inflorescence:** the main axis **terminates in a flower**, hence is limited in growth; the flowers are borne in a **basipetal order**.
groundedIn: §5.4; Fig. 5.7; Fig. 5.8 — inflorescence: arrangement of flowers on the floral axis; depending on whether the apex develops into a flower or continues to grow, racemose (acropetal) and cymose (basipetal)

stem: Describe the arrangement of floral members in relation to their insertion on thalamus.
solution:
Based on the position of calyx, corolla and androecium in respect of the ovary on the thalamus, flowers are of three types:

1. **Hypogynous:** the gynoecium occupies the **highest position** and the other parts are situated below it. The ovary is **superior**. Examples: mustard, china rose and brinjal.
2. **Perigynous:** the gynoecium is situated in the centre and the other parts are located on the **rim of the thalamus** almost at the same level. The ovary is **half inferior**. Examples: plum, rose, peach.
3. **Epigynous:** the margin of the thalamus grows upward, **enclosing the ovary completely** and getting fused with it; the other parts arise **above the ovary**. The ovary is **inferior**. Examples: guava, cucumber and the ray florets of sunflower.
groundedIn: §5.5; Fig. 5.9 — hypogynous (superior ovary: mustard, china rose, brinjal), perigynous (half inferior: plum, rose, peach), epigynous (inferior: guava, cucumber, ray florets of sunflower)
